300	**Design notes for Task 2.**
301	
302	*Why scan for terminators instead of splitting on a regular expression.* A split such as `text.split(/[.!?]+/)` cannot ask "was the word before this period an abbreviation?" The scan walks the matches, keeps the start of the current segment, and decides at each terminator whether the segment ends there. Skipping a terminator simply leaves the segment start where it was, so `Mr. Smith went.` is one segment.
303	
304	*Why require whitespace or the end of the text after a terminator.* It is the cheapest rule that keeps decimals, versions (`v1.2.3`), domains and `a.b.c` in one piece without a list of exceptions. Its cost is text with no space after a period, such as `Hello.World`, which counts as one sentence. Prose in the wild nearly always has the space, and the reference table records the choice.
305	
306	*Why closing quotes and brackets belong to the terminator.* In `"Stop!" she said.` the exclamation mark ends the quoted sentence, and the closing quote that follows must not turn the next character into the start of a new run. Including the closers in the match means the terminator is found where the whitespace begins. It also makes `(Done.) Next.` two sentences, which matches how a reader splits it.
307	
308	*Why abbreviations are checked only for a lone period.* `Mr..` or `Dr?` are not abbreviations, and a question mark after `Dr` is a real sentence end. Checking `match[1] === '.'` keeps the abbreviation rule from swallowing a legitimate break.
309	
310	*Why the abbreviation list is short.* Each entry is a bet that the word is more often an abbreviation than a sentence-final word. `St.`, `Sr.` and `Jr.` are borderline and stay because the false break is more disruptive than the missed one in ordinary prose. 313	
314	*Why the `for ... of` over `matchAll`.* `String.prototype.matchAll` clones the regular expression, so the module-level pattern's `lastIndex` is never shared between calls. That is what lets the pattern live at module scope without any state leaking from one call to the next, which the Conventions section forbids.

1	**Tech Stack:** Node.js 20 (`node:test`, `node:assert/strict`), CommonJS modules, no runtime or dev dependencies. The suite runs with `npm test`, which is `node --test`.
2	
3	## Conventions
4	
5	These apply to every task below. They are written down once so each task can stay short on process and long on content.
6	
7	- **Module format.** CommonJS (`require` / `module.exports`). `package.json` has no `type` field, and this plan never adds one.
8	- **Test files.** One file per function, named `test/<functionName>.test.js`, using `const { test } = require('node:test');` and `const assert = require('node:assert/strict');`. Test names are full sentences in the present tense that say what the function does ("counts hyphenated compounds as one word"), never "test 1".
9	- **Red before green.** Every task writes its test file first, runs `npm test`, and sees it fail for the stated reason before any implementation is written. A test that has never failed has not shown that it can.
10	- **Argument validation.** Text arguments must be strings. A non-string throws `TypeError` whose message starts with the function name and a colon. Numeric arguments that are out of range throw `RangeError` with the same prefix. Tests assert on the error class and on the message prefix, never on the full message text.
11	- **No state.** None of the functions mutates its arguments, caches results, or reads anything from the environment. Calling a function twice with the same arguments returns equal values.
12	- **Commits.** One commit per task, conventional prefix `feat:`, message in the imperative, and the test file and implementation in the same commit. Do not commit while `npm test` is red.
13	- **Scope.** English prose only. Right-to-left scripts, languages without spaces between words, and markup stripping are out of scope; the notes in each task name the specific cases that are deliberately left alone.

7	`sentenceCount` splits prose at sentence terminators while avoiding the three most common false breaks: decimal numbers, dotted names such as `example.com`, and abbreviations like `Mr.` and `e.g.`. It reuses `tokenize` and `assertText` from Task 1 and appends to `src/textstats.js` without changing anything already there.

9	**Behaviour.**
10	
11	- A terminator is a run of `.`, `!` or `?` (so `?!` and `...` are one terminator), optionally followed by closing quotes or brackets, and only when whitespace or the end of the text follows it. A period inside `3.14`, `example.com` or `a.b.c` has no whitespace after it and is not a terminator.

13	- A sentence is counted only if it contains at least one word, so a text made only of terminators has zero sentences.
14	- Text after the last terminator counts as a final sentence when it contains a word.

241	// only where whitespace or the end of the text follows. Requiring that keeps

300	**Design notes for Task 2.**
301	
302	*Why scan for terminators instead of splitting on a regular expression.* A split such as `text.split(/[.!?]+/)` cannot ask "was the word before this period an abbreviation?" The scan walks the matches, keeps the start of the current segment, and decides at each terminator whether the segment ends there. Skipping a terminator simply leaves the segment start where it was, so `Mr. Smith went.` is one segment.
303	
304	*Why require whitespace or the end of the text after a terminator.* It is the cheapest rule that keeps decimals, versions (`v1.2.3`), domains and `a.b.c` in one piece without a list of exceptions. Its cost is text with no space after a period, such as `Hello.World`, which counts as one sentence. Prose in the wild nearly always has the space, and the reference table records the choice.
305	
306	*Why closing quotes and brackets belong to the terminator.* In `"Stop!" she said.` the exclamation mark ends the quoted sentence, and the closing quote that follows must not turn the next character into the start of a new run. Including the closers in the match means the terminator is found where the whitespace begins. It also makes `(Done.) Next.` two sentences, which matches how a reader splits it.
307	
308	*Why abbreviations are checked only for a lone period.* `Mr..` or `Dr?` are not abbreviations, and a question mark after `Dr` is a real sentence end. Checking `match[1] === '.'` keeps the abbreviation rule from swallowing a legitimate break.
309	
310	*Why the abbreviation list is short.* Each entry is a bet that the word is more often an abbreviation than a sentence-final word. `St.`, `Sr.` and `Jr.` are borderline and stay because the false break is more disruptive than the missed one in ordinary prose. Initialisms such as `U.S.A.` stay off the list because they are as likely to end a sentence as not, and the reference table pins the resulting count.
311	
312	*Why `tokenize` decides whether a segment counts.* A segment of `...` or of a lone quotation mark has no words, and counting it would make `sentenceCount('...')` return one. Reusing `tokenize` keeps the definition of "contains a word" identical to Task 1's.
313	
314	*Why the `for ... of` over `matchAll`.* `String.prototype.matchAll` clones the regular expression, so the module-level pattern's `lastIndex` is never shared between calls. That is what lets the pattern live at module scope without any state leaking from one call to the next, which the Conventions section forbids.

316	**Known limitations of Task 2.**

318	- A sentence that genuinely ends with one of the listed abbreviations (`He moved to St. Louis` is fine, but `We stayed at the inn on Main St. Then we left.`) is merged with the next sentence.

278	**Design notes for Task 3.**
279	
280	*Why the stop-word list is fixed and short.* A configurable list would need a third argument, and the signature in this plan is `topWords(text, n)`. A caller who wants a different list can ask for a large `n` and filter the result. The 36 words chosen are the ones that dominate a ranking of English prose; the list is not meant to be linguistically complete.
281	
282	*Why stop words are removed after case and apostrophe folding.* `The`, `THE` and `the` must all be skipped, and so must a stop word that arrives with a typographic apostrophe. Folding first and testing the folded form means the list needs only lower-case, straight-apostrophe entries. None of the 36 entries contains an apostrophe, so contractions such as `it's` and `they're` are not stop words and appear in rankings. The reference table pins that.
283	
284	*Why `toLowerCase` and not `toLocaleLowerCase`.* The result must not depend on the host locale. In a Turkish locale `toLocaleLowerCase` turns `I` into a dotless `ı`, which would split `It` and `it`. `toLowerCase` applies the locale-independent Unicode mapping. The one visible consequence is that `ß` stays `ß` and is a different word from `ss`, which the reference table records.
285	
286	*Why the comparator avoids `localeCompare`.* The same locale argument applies. Comparing with `<` orders by UTF-16 code unit: `strasse` sorts before `straße` because `s` (U+0073) is less than `ß` (U+00DF). The ordering is not linguistically perfect but is identical on every machine, which is what a test suite needs.
287	
288	*Why validate `n` strictly.* `slice(0, undefined)` returns everything, `slice(0, -1)` drops the last element, and `slice(0, 1.5)` truncates silently. Each of those hides a caller mistake. Requiring a non-negative integer turns all of them into an immediate `RangeError`. Zero is allowed because "no entries" is a legitimate request and keeps loops over `n` simple.
289	
290	*Why a `Map` and not a plain object.* A plain object would treat the word `constructor` or `__proto__` specially. A `Map` has no such keys, so every word is safe. The ranking is built from `[...counts]`, which preserves insertion order until the sort.
291	
292	*Why fresh objects.* The result objects are created in the `map` step on every call, so there is nothing shared to leak. The test named "returns fresh objects on every call" guards against a later optimisation that caches rankings.
293	
294	**Known limitations of Task 3.**
295	
296	- No stemming: `walk` and `walking` are different words.
297	- No lemmatisation of contractions: `it's` is its own word and not `it`.
298	- The stop-word list is English only.
299	- Case folding is not full Unicode case folding: `Straße` and `STRASSE` stay apart.

1	**Tech Stack:** Node.js 20 (`node:test`, `node:assert/strict`), CommonJS modules, no runtime or dev dependencies. The suite runs with `npm test`, which is `node --test`.
2	
3	## Conventions
4	
5	These apply to every task below. They are written down once so each task can stay short on process and long on content.
6	
7	- **Module format.** CommonJS (`require` / `module.exports`). `package.json` has no `type` field, and this plan never adds one.
8	- **Test files.** One file per function, named `test/<functionName>.test.js`, using `const { test } = require('node:test');` and `const assert = require('node:assert/strict');`. Test names are full sentences in the present tense that say what the function does ("counts hyphenated compounds as one word"), never "test 1".
9	- **Red before green.** Every task writes its test file first, runs `npm test`, and sees it fail for the stated reason before any implementation is written. A test that has never failed has not shown that it can.
10	- **Argument validation.** Text arguments must be strings. A non-string throws `TypeError` whose message starts with the function name and a colon. Numeric arguments that are out of range throw `RangeError` with the same prefix. Tests assert on the error class and on the message prefix, never on the full message text.
11	- **No state.** None of the functions mutates its arguments, caches results, or reads anything from the environment. Calling a function twice with the same arguments returns equal values.
12	- **Commits.** One commit per task, conventional prefix `feat:`, message in the imperative, and the test file and implementation in the same commit. Do not commit while `npm test` is red.
13	- **Scope.** English prose only. Right-to-left scripts, languages without spaces between words, and markup stripping are out of scope; the notes in each task name the specific cases that are deliberately left alone.

The 36 words chosen are the ones that dominate a ranking of English prose; the list is not meant to be linguistically complete.

*Why stop words are removed after case and apostrophe folding.* `The`, `THE` and `the` must all be skipped, and so must a stop word that arrives with a typographic apostrophe. Folding first and testing the folded form means the list needs only lower-case, straight-apostrophe entries. None of the 36 entries contains an apostrophe, so contractions such as `it's` and `they're` are not stop words and appear in rankings. The reference table pins that.

*Why `toLowerCase` and not `toLocaleLowerCase`.* The result must not depend on the host locale. In a Turkish locale `toLocaleLowerCase` turns `I` into a dotless `ı`, which would split `It` and `it`. `toLowerCase` applies the locale-independent Unicode mapping. The one visible consequence is that `ß` stays `ß` and is a different word from `ss`, which the reference table records.

*Why the comparator avoids `localeCompare`.* The same locale argument applies. Comparing with `<` orders by UTF-16 code unit: `strasse` sorts before `straße` because `s` (U+0073) is less than `ß` (U+00DF). The ordering is not linguistically perfect but is identical on every machine, which is what a test suite needs.

*Why validate `n` strictly.* `slice(0, undefined)` returns everything, `slice(0, -1)` drops the last element, and `slice(0, 1.5)` truncates silently. Each of those hides a caller mistake. Requiring a non-negative integer turns all of them into an immediate `RangeError`. Zero is allowed because "no entries" is a legitimate request and keeps loops over `n` simple.

*Why a `Map` and not a plain object.* A plain object would treat the word `constructor` or `__proto__` specially. A `Map` has no such keys, so every word is safe. The ranking is built from `[...counts]`, which preserves insertion order until the sort.

*Why fresh objects.* The result objects are created in the `map` step on every call, so there is nothing shared to leak. The test named "returns fresh objects on every call" guards against a later optimisation that caches rankings.

222	**Design notes for Task 4.**
223	
224	*Why round up.* A reader who needs 30 seconds still opens the page for a whole minute, and "0 min read" on a short but non-empty text is a worse label than "1 min read". Rounding up with `Math.ceil` also gives the exact boundaries the tests pin: 200 words is one minute and 201 is two.
225	
226	*Why the empty text is zero and not one.* `Math.ceil(0 / 200)` is `0`. The function reports what the text needs, and a text with no words needs no time. A caller who wants a floor of one minute can apply `Math.max(1, ...)`.
227	
228	*Why validate `wpm` after the text.* Both checks throw, so the order only matters for which error a caller sees when both arguments are wrong. Checking the text first matches the other three functions, where the text is always the first argument examined.
229	
230	*Why reject numeric strings.* `'200'` would work arithmetically, since `5 / '200'` is a number, but accepting it hides a caller who read a rate from a form and never parsed it. The check requires `typeof wpm === 'number'`, so that mistake surfaces as a `RangeError`.

# Code Reviewer Prompt Template

Use this template when dispatching a code reviewer subagent.

**Purpose:** Review completed work against requirements and code quality standards before it cascades into more work.

```
Subagent (general-purpose):
  description: "Review code changes"
  prompt: |
    You are a Senior Code Reviewer with expertise in software architecture,
    design patterns, and best practices. Your job is to review completed work
    against its plan or requirements and identify issues before they cascade.

    ## What Was Implemented

    [DESCRIPTION]

    ## Requirements / Plan

    [PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS]

    ## Git Range to Review

    **Base:** [BASE_SHA]
    **Head:** [HEAD_SHA]

    ```bash
    git diff --stat [BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]
    git diff [BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]
    ```

    ## Read-Only Review

    Your review is read-only on this checkout. Do not mutate the working tree, the index, HEAD, or branch state in any way. Use tools like `git show`, `git diff`, and `git log` to inspect history. If you need a working copy of a different revision, check it out into a separate temporary directory (e.g. `git worktree add /tmp/review-[SHA] [SHA]`) — never move HEAD on this checkout.

    Do all of this review yourself. Never spawn a subagent to review part

...

    - Acknowledge strengths

    **DON'T:**

    - Be vague ("improve error handling")

```

# Textstats Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use hyperpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or hyperpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Spec:** none (fixture)

**Goal:** Build `textstats`, a small dependency-free Node.js module that reports four statistics about a piece of English prose: the number of words, the number of sentences, the most frequent words, and an estimated reading time.

**Architecture:** One CommonJS module, `src/textstats.js`, exports four pure functions. A private `tokenize` helper (added in Task 1) is the single definition of what a "word" is; `wordCount`, `topWords` and `readingTimeMinutes` all build on it so the three numbers can never disagree about the text. `sentenceCount` (Task 2) uses its own terminator scan and borrows `tokenize` only to decide whether a segment holds any words at all. Every function validates its arguments and throws a `TypeError` or `RangeError` with a message naming the function, rather than returning a silent wrong answer. Each function has its own test file under `test/`, so a failing statistic points at one file.

**Tech Stack:** Node.js 20 (`node:test`, `node:assert/strict`), CommonJS modules, no runtime or dev dependencies. The suite runs with `npm test`, which is `node --test`.

## Conventions

These apply to every task below. They are written down once so each task can stay short on process and long on content.

- **Module format.** CommonJS (`require` / `module.exports`). `package.json` has no `type` field, and this plan never adds one.
- **Test files.** One file per function, named `test/<functionName>.test.js`, using `const { test } = require('node:test');` and `const assert = require('node:assert/strict');`. Test names are full sentences in the present tense that say what the function does ("counts hyphenated compounds as one word"), never "test 1".
- **Red before green.** Every task writes its test file first, runs `npm test`, and sees it fail for the stated reason before any implementation is written. A test that has never failed has not shown that it can.
- **Argument validation.** Text arguments must be strings. A non-string throws `TypeError` whose message starts with the function name and a colon. Numeric arguments that are out of range throw `RangeError` with the same prefix. Tests assert on the error class and on the message prefix, never on the full message text.
- **No state.** None of the functions mutates its arguments, caches results, or reads anything from the environment. Calling a function twice with the same arguments returns equal values.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/johnss51/.cache/hyperpowers/cost-6162/hp-6161/skills/finishing-a-development-branch

# Finishing a Development Branch

## Overview

**Core principle:** Verify tests → Detect environment → Present options → Execute choice → Clean up.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for the test-failure report and the PR description. The option menus below are presented exactly as written.

## Step 1: Verify Tests

Run the project's full test suite (`npm test` / `cargo test` / `pytest` / `go test ./...`).

**If tests fail**, report the failures and stop — the menu comes after a green suite:

```
Tests failing (<N> failures). Must fix before completing:

[Show failures]
```

**If tests pass:** continue to Step 2.

## Step 2: Detect Environment

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
# Capture now, while still inside the workspace — Step 5 changes directory
# before cleanup (Step 6) needs this value
WORKTREE_PATH=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
```

This determines which menu to show and how cleanup works:

| State | Menu | Cleanup |
|-------|------|---------|
| `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON` (normal repo) | Standard 3 options | No worktree to clean up |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, named branch | Standard 3 options | Provenance-based (see Step 6) |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, detached HEAD | Reduced 2 options (no merge) | Externally managed — leave in place |

## Step 3: Determine Base Branch

The base branch is whatever this work forked from — usually named in the
plan, the conversation, or the branch's upstream. If it is not already
known, ask: "This branch split from <your best guess> - is that correct?"
Confirm before merging: merging into the wrong base is expensive to undo.

## Step 4: Present Options

**Normal repo and named-branch worktree — present exactly these 3 options:**

```
Implementation complete. What would you like to do?

1. Merge back to <base-branch> locally
2. Push and create a Pull Request
3. Keep the branch as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

**Detached HEAD — present exactly these 2 options:**

```
Implementation complete. You're on a detached HEAD (externally managed workspace).

1. Push as new branch and create a Pull Request
2. Keep as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

Present the menu exactly as written — concise, with every option coming
from the list above. Discarding the work happens only in response to your
human partner explicitly asking for it (see "If your human partner asks to
discard the work" below). Wait for their answer; the integration decision
is theirs.

## Step 5: Execute Choice

### Option 1: Merge Locally

```bash
# Get main repo root for CWD safety
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"

# Merge first — verify success before removing anything
git checkout <base-branch>
git pull
git merge <feature-branch>

# Verify tests on merged result
<test command>
```

If tests fail on the merged result: stop, leave the worktree and branch in
place, and investigate — nothing has been pushed, so the merge is local
and recoverable.

Once the merged result is green: clean up the worktree (Step 6), then
delete the branch:

```bash
git branch -d <feature-branch>
```

### Option 2: Push and Create PR

```bash
git push -u origin <feature-branch>
# From a detached HEAD, name the new branch on the remote:
# git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/<new-branch>
```

Then create the pull/merge request against <base-branch> with the forge's
tooling — its CLI if one is available, or the creation URL most forges
print when you push — following the repo's PR template and conventions if
present, and report the URL to your human partner.

Keep the worktree — your human partner iterates on PR feedback there.

### Option 3: Keep As-Is

Report: "Keeping branch <name>. Worktree preserved at <path>."

### If your human partner asks to discard the work

This path exists only as a response to an explicit request to throw the
work away. Confirm first:

```
This will permanently delete:
- Branch <name>
- All commits: <commit-list>
- Worktree at <path>

Type 'discard' to confirm.
```

Wait for that exact confirmation. When it arrives:

```bash
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"
```

Then clean up the worktree (Step 6) and force-delete the branch:

```bash
git branch -D <feature-branch>
```

## Step 6: Cleanup Workspace

**Runs for Option 1 and confirmed discards.** Options 2 and 3 always
preserve the worktree. Both callers have already changed directory to the
main repo root — worktree removal must run from outside the worktree —
and use the `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_COMMON`/`WORKTREE_PATH` values captured in
Step 2, from before that directory change.

**If `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON`:** Normal repo, no worktree to clean up. Done.

**If `WORKTREE_PATH` is under `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/`:** Superpowers
created this worktree — we own cleanup:

```bash
git worktree remove "$WORKTREE_PATH"
git worktree prune  # Self-healing: clean up any stale registrations
```

**If removal is refused** (`contains modified or untracked files`): the
worktree holds files that exist nowhere else — uncommitted plans, notes,
or scratch work. Never `--force` on your own initiative. Show your human
partner what is at stake and ask:

```bash
git -C "$WORKTREE_PATH" status --porcelain -uall
```

```
Worktree removal refused — these files were never committed:

<file list>

1. Commit them to <branch> before cleanup
2. Move them into <main repo root>
3. Delete them (unrecoverable)

Which?
```

Carry out the choice, then remove the worktree.

**Otherwise:** The host environment owns this workspace — leave it in
place. If your platform provides a workspace-exit tool, use it.

## Quick Reference

| Option | Merge | Push | Keep Worktree | Cleanup Branch |
|--------|-------|------|---------------|----------------|
| 1. Merge locally | yes | - | - | yes |
| 2. Create PR | - | yes | yes | - |
| 3. Keep as-is | - | - | yes | - |
| Discard (explicit request only) | - | - | - | yes (force) |

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Tests passed earlier this session" | Run the suite on the tree you are about to integrate. A green run only proves the tree it ran on. |
| "They obviously want it merged" | Integration is your human partner's decision. Present the menu and wait. |
| "They seem done with this feature — I'll offer to discard it" | The menu is complete as written. Discard happens only when your human partner asks for it in so many words. |
| "'Yeah, get rid of it' counts as confirmation" | Only the typed word `discard` authorizes deletion. |
| "The PR is up, so the worktree is clutter now" | PR feedback gets fixed in that worktree. It stays until the work lands. |
| "This other worktree looks stale — I'll clean it too" | Clean up only worktrees under `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/`. Everything else belongs to the host. |
| "Removal refused — `--force` is just finishing the cleanup" | The refusal means files exist only in that worktree. `--force` destroys them permanently. Show your human partner and ask. |
| "The merged-result failure is probably flaky" | A failing merged result stops everything. Branch and worktree stay put while you investigate. |
| "The base branch is obviously main" | Confirm the fork point or ask. Merging into the wrong base is expensive to undo. |
| "The push was rejected — force-push will fix it" | A rejected push means the remote moved. Investigate; force-push only on your human partner's explicit request. |
